    Enterprise AI Security

    Enterprise AI Security: a practical guide for regulated organizations

    Employees in legal, fintech and healthcare are already using LLMs at work. This guide covers the threat model, the essential controls and a rollout plan you can execute in weeks — not quarters.

    The threat model

    Enterprise AI security is not a model problem — it is a data-flow problem. Sensitive data leaves the organization the moment an employee pastes it into ChatGPT, Claude or an internal agent. Once inside a provider's logs or training pipeline, it is out of your control.

    • Prompt leakage — PII, contracts and secrets pasted into public LLMs.
    • Agent-to-agent handoffs — one agent forwards sensitive context to another without policy checks.
    • Embedding drift — sensitive strings preserved in vector databases far longer than expected.
    • Third-party plugins — tool calls that exfiltrate data outside your perimeter.

    Essential controls

    1. Detection — hybrid regex + NLP models to identify PII, financial data and contracts in every prompt.
    2. Policy enforcement — tokenize, anonymize or block based on role, org and provider.

    RAG & Knowledge Base Protection

    Keep PII out of your RAG pipeline
    before it's indexed, and before it's retrieved

    Privaro Ingest protects documents before they enter your vector store. Privaro Retrieval Guard protects retrieved chunks before they reach your LLM's context — even for knowledge bases indexed before you added Privaro.

    Request DemoRead the docs

    Two layers, one pipeline

    Ingestion-time protection and retrieval-time protection cover different failure modes — most teams need both.

    Protect before indexing

    Send raw text or upload a file directly — PDF, Word, Excel, CSV or email. Privaro extracts the text, detects PII, and returns a tokenized version ready to embed.

    Protect at retrieval time

    Scan chunks returned by your vector store search before they're stuffed into an LLM prompt — a second layer of defense that catches PII even in knowledge bases indexed without protection.

    Per-chunk access control

    Restrict specific chunks to specific roles. A chunk tagged for finance never reaches a support agent's context, regardless of what the vector search returns.

    Content-hash caching

    The same chunk retrieved repeatedly is only scanned once. Cached by content, not by your own chunk ID — re-indexed content still benefits.

    Ingest a document — text or file

    Paste text directly, or upload a file up to 20MB. Documents over roughly 20,000 characters are processed asynchronously — poll the job endpoint for the result.

    POST https://api.privaro.ai/v1/proxy/protect-document
X-Privaro-Key: YOUR_API_KEY
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "pipeline_id": "YOUR_PIPELINE_ID",
  "document": "Full document text — up to 2,000,000 characters",
  "options": { "mode": "tokenise", "chunk_size": 512 }
}

// Response (documents under ~20,000 characters — synchronous)
{
  "status": "completed",
  "protected_document": "...",
  "chunks": [
    { "index": 0, "text": "...", "char_start": 0, "char_end": 511 }
  ],
  "detections": [ ... ],
  "stats": { "total_detected": 12, "chunk_count": 8, "processing_ms": 340 }
}

    Upload documents directly, or send extracted text yourself — whichever fits your pipeline.

    PDF
    DOCX
    XLSX
    CSV
    EML
    Plain text
    POST https://api.privaro.ai/v1/proxy/protect-document/upload
X-Privaro-Key: YOUR_API_KEY
Content-Type: multipart/form-data

file: report.pdf
pipeline_id: YOUR_PIPELINE_ID
mode: tokenise

// Same response shape as the text endpoint above —
// PDF, DOCX, XLSX, CSV and EML are extracted server-side.

    Guard what reaches the model at query time

    Send a batch of retrieved chunks along with the requester's role. Chunks that fail access control or PII detection never make it into your prompt.

    POST https://api.privaro.ai/v1/proxy/protect-retrieval
X-Privaro-Key: YOUR_API_KEY
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "pipeline_id": "YOUR_PIPELINE_ID",
  "chunks": [
    { "id": "chunk_123", "text": "...", "allowed_roles": ["finance"] },
    { "id": "chunk_456", "text": "..." }
  ],
  "requester": { "role": "support-agent" }
}

// Response
{
  "allowed_chunks": [
    { "id": "chunk_456", "protected_text": "...", "from_cache": false }

    { "id": "chunk_123", "reason": "access_denied" }

    🔒 Security & Compliance

    Enterprise-grade security
    by design, not by policy

    Privaro's privacy infrastructure is built on the principle that security controls must be architectural — not application-layer afterthoughts.

    AES-256-GCM EncryptionBlockchain-Certified Audit TrailGDPR Art.5 CompliantTLS 1.3 EnforcedSOC2 Type I — In PreparationISO 27001 — In Preparation

    Architecture

    Security built into every layer

    Privacy controls are applied at the network layer — before any data reaches an AI model. This is architecturally superior to post-processing or application-level filtering.

    🔐

    Zero Raw PII Exposure

    No plaintext personal data is ever transmitted to an AI provider. Tokenization occurs within Privaro's trusted boundary. Original values are stored exclusively in the encrypted vault.

    ⛓️

    Verifiable Compliance Evidence

    Audit records are cryptographically certified on Fantom Opera Mainnet. Compliance is demonstrable to regulators independently of Privaro's infrastructure.

    🛡️

    Defense in Depth

    Security controls are layered: TLS 1.3 at the network level, JWT + API key auth at the application level, Row Level Security at the database level, AES-256-GCM at the data level.

    ⚙️

    Policy-Driven Governance

    Every entity type has a configurable action: tokenise, anonymise, or block. Sector presets for Legal, Healthcare, Fintech, HR, and Port Environmental are built-in.

    🤖

    Agent Governance

    Autonomous AI agents operate under the same privacy policies as human users. The Agent API enforces governance at every step of automated workflows — EU AI Act compliant.

    🌍

    Agent Step Privacy

    Every agent step is intercepted before reaching the LLM. PII is detected and tokenised per step, not per session. Each interaction generates an iBS blockchain certificate — immutable proof of what the agent processed and what the model never saw.

    🔑

    BYOK — Bring Your Own Key

    Enterprise clients manage their own encryption keys. Privaro never stores key material — only a secure reference. Keys can be rotated, revoked, and audited independently per organisation via the admin panel.

    Controls

    Implemented security controls

    Key technical controls aligned to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A and SOC2 Trust Services Criteria.

    NLP Privacy Engine

    Two-tier detection pipeline

    Combines deterministic regex with neural NLP models to maximise recall on structured PII and precision on unstructured entities.

    Tier 1 — Regex

    Deterministic detection of structured PII: DNI/NIE, IBAN, credit cards, phone numbers, emails, IPs, passport numbers. Zero false negatives on known formats.

    Tier 2 — Neural NLP

    Context-aware detection of unstructured PII: full names, organisations, locations, dates. Confidence threshold ≥0.75 with post-NLP filters to eliminate false positives in legal and technical documents.

    Agent Step Mode

    Every agent step runs through the full detection pipeline before reaching the LLM. PII is tokenised, the step is certified on blockchain, and an iBS signature is generated per interaction — not per session.

    Compliance guide

    EU AI Act: a practical compliance guide

    The European AI Act is already in force and its obligations land in phases through 2027. This guide covers what applies to you depending on how you use AI, on which dates, what the fines are, and what you need documented before anyone asks for it.

    Updated: September 2026

    Assess your risk in 3 minutesDownload the guide as PDFSee how Privaro helps

    What the EU AI Act is and who it applies to

    Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 is the world's first comprehensive law on artificial intelligence. It does not regulate the technology in the abstract: it regulates uses. Every AI system is classified by the risk it poses to people's rights, with obligations proportional to that risk.

    It applies to providers placing AI systems on the EU market and to organisations deploying them in their operations, whether or not they are established in the EU, as long as the output is used within the Union. In practice: if your team uses an LLM to process European customer data, it affects you, even when the model belongs to someone else.

    Key dates

    Obligations do not arrive all at once. This is the official application timeline.

    1. 1 August 2024

      Entry into force

      The Regulation enters into force and starts the clock on every later deadline.

    2. 2 February 2025

      Prohibited practices and AI literacy

      Uses such as social scoring and untargeted facial scraping become banned. Organisations must also ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among their staff.

    3. 2 August 2025

      General-purpose AI models (GPAI)

      Transparency, technical documentation and copyright-policy duties for foundation model providers. Governance rules and penalties start to apply.

    4. 2 August 2026

      General application

      The bulk of the Regulation applies, including Annex III high-risk systems and transparency duties for systems interacting with people.

    5. 2 August 2027

      High-risk embedded in products

      Applies to AI systems that are safety components of products already covered by other Union legislation (Annex I).

    The four risk tiers

    Your first compliance task is classifying every AI system you use correctly.

    Unacceptable risk

    What it covers

    Social scoring, subliminal manipulation, emotion recognition at work or school, biometric categorisation using sensitive traits.

    What it requires

    Banned. There is no mitigation available: the use must stop.

    High risk

    What it covers

    Recruitment, credit scoring, education, essential services, justice, migration, and AI acting as a product safety component.

    What it requires

    Risk management system, data governance, technical documentation, automatic event logging, human oversight, accuracy and cybersecurity, plus registration in the EU database.

    Transparency risk

    What it covers

    Chatbots, content generators, deepfakes, systems interacting directly with people.

    What it requires

    Tell users they are interacting with an AI and label generated or manipulated content in a machine-readable way.

    Minimal risk

    What it covers

    Spam filters, video games, internal recommenders and most office use cases.

    What it requires

    No specific obligations. Voluntary codes of conduct are encouraged.

    Fines

    • Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of global annual turnover for engaging in prohibited practices.
    • Up to EUR 15 million or 3% for breaching high-risk, transparency or GPAI obligations.
    • Up to EUR 7.5 million or 1% for supplying incorrect or misleading information to authorities.

    Compliance checklist

    Ten concrete steps you can start today, ordered by what regulators ask for first.

    1

    Inventory every AI system

    Include the ones you did not buy as AI: assistants inside your CRM, code copilots, meeting transcribers. What is not inventoried cannot be governed.

    2

    Classify each system by risk tier

    Document the reasoning, not just the conclusion. Justifying why something is not high risk matters as much as the classification itself.

    3

    Establish your role in each case

    Providers and deployers carry very different duties. Fine-tuning a model on your own data can turn you into a provider.

    4

    Evidence your team's AI literacy

    Mandatory since February 2025. Record who received what training and when.

    5

    Set up data governance

    Which data enters each system, where it comes from, on what legal basis, and what happens to sensitive data before it reaches a model.

    6

    Log every AI interaction

    The Regulation requires automatic event traceability for high-risk systems. A record of who asked what, to which model, with which data, is your baseline evidence.

    7

    Design human oversight

    Define who can review, correct or reverse an AI-assisted decision, and show they genuinely can.

    8

    Meet user-facing transparency

    Disclose when someone is talking to an AI and label generated content. These are the easiest duties to check from the outside.

    9

    Review contracts with model providers

    Data retention, training use, processing location and sub-processors. Their failures end up being yours.

    10

    Build the evidence file

    Technical documentation, risk assessments, logs and incidents in one exportable place. Conformity is demonstrated, not declared.

    Where Privaro fits

    Privaro does not deliver compliance on its own: it covers the technical part that is hardest to improvise, which is controlling and proving what data leaves for the models.

    Detects personal and sensitive data in every prompt before it reaches the model.
    Applies policies by data type, team and provider: tokenize, anonymize or block.
    Logs every interaction with user, model, detected entities and the decision applied.
    Scans model responses too, catching data leaks on the way out.
    Exports audit-ready reports for your data protection officer.
    Works with OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini and others without changing your integration.

    Frequently asked questions

    Does the EU AI Act apply if my company is outside the EU?

    Yes, if the system's output is used within the Union or you place the system on the EU market. The test is where the effect happens, not where you are headquartered.

    Does using ChatGPT at work make me an AI provider?

    Usually not: you would be a deployer, with lighter duties. But if you fine-tune the model, ship it under your own brand or substantially change its intended purpose, you can become a provider and take on the full set of obligations.

    Does the EU AI Act replace GDPR?

    No, they stack. GDPR still governs personal data processing while the AI Act adds duties about the AI system itself. One use case can breach both independently.

    What if I use streaming responses and cannot mask the output?

    With streaming, the output is audited in real time rather than masked. The detection is recorded for evidence and alerting even though the text already reached the user. Document that limitation in your risk assessment.

    Official sources

    Integrate Privaro in under an hour

    Detect and tokenise PII before it reaches any LLM. One endpoint change — no architecture rewrite.

    1

    Get your API key

    Sign up and create your account. Your API key will be available in the dashboard under Settings → API Keys. It starts with prvr_.

    Create your account
    2

    Install the SDK

    Choose your stack. The SDK has zero runtime dependencies.

    bash
    npm install privaro-sdk
    3

    Create a pipeline

    A pipeline defines which LLM provider you use and which policy rules apply. Create one in the dashboard, then copy its UUID.

    bashInstructions — not code to run
    # In your dashboard: /app/pipelines → New pipeline
# Choose your LLM provider and configure policy rules
# Copy the pipeline UUID from the pipeline detail page
    4

    Protect your first prompt

    Pass any text through Privaro before sending it to your LLM. PII is detected and replaced with reversible tokens.

    typescript
    import { PrivaroClient } from "privaro-sdk";

const privaro = new PrivaroClient({
  apiKey: process.env.PRIVARO_API_KEY,
  pipelineId: process.env.PRIVARO_PIPELINE_ID,
});

const result = await privaro.protect(
  "Solicitante: Laura Sánchez (DNI: 23456789D) " +
  "Email: laura@empresa.com · IBAN: ES98 2100 0418 6819 6340 7321"
);

console.log(result.protected);
// "Solicitante: [NM-0001] (DNI: [ID-0001]) "
// "Email: [EM-0001] · IBAN: [BK-0001]"

console.log(result.summary());
// [Privaro] 4 detected, 4 masked, risk=high, gdpr=✓, 48ms
    5

    Send the protected prompt to your LLM

    Use result.protected instead of the original prompt. Your LLM never sees real PII — only tokens like [NM-0001] and [ID-0001].

    typescript
    // Send the protected prompt to your LLM
const response = await openai.chat.completions.create({
  model: "gpt-4o",
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: result.protected }],
});
// LLM never sees the real PII — only tokens like [NM-0001]

    Building a RAG pipeline? The three steps above cover single-turn chat protection. Document ingestion and retrieval-time protection follow a different flow — see the dedicated RAG protection guide for accurate, working code samples.

    What you get out of the box

    Hybrid detection

    Tier 1 regex (deterministic) + Tier 2 Presidio NLP (contextual). 10 entity types including DNI, IBAN, phone, full name, and health records.

    Under 60 ms

    P95 latency across all pipelines. Privaro adds less than 60 ms to your existing LLM call — invisible to the end user.

    GDPR-ready audit trail

    Every request writes an audit log entry certified on iCommunity Blockchain. Exportable as PDF for DPO reports and EU AI Act compliance.

    API reference

    Base URL: https://api.privaro.ai/v1

    POST
    /proxy/protect

    Detect and tokenise PII. Writes audit log + iBS blockchain certification.

    POST
    /proxy/detect

    Detect PII without masking. Analysis mode — no state written.

    POST
    /relay/complete

    Full-cycle relay: protect → route to configured LLM → de-tokenise response.

    POST
    /agent/reveal

    Replace tokens with original values in a text. Requires conversationId.

    POST
    /relay/stream

    Streaming relay (SSE). Each delta is returned already de-tokenised. Output is audited in real time but not masked — chunks are delivered as they are produced.

    POST
    /proxy/protect-output

    Scan and mask the response text from your own LLM. Use it when you call /proxy/protect and then your model directly. Requires output_scanning_enabled on the pipeline.

    POST
    /proxy/protect-document

    Protect a text document — paste up to 2,000,000 characters directly. Same detection engine as /proxy/protect. Synchronous under ~20,000 characters; above that, returns a job_id to poll.

    POST
    /proxy/protect-document/upload

    Protect a document by uploading a file directly — PDF, Word, Excel, CSV or email, up to 20MB. Extracts the text server-side and masks it with the same detection engine.

    GET
    /proxy/protect-document/{job_id}

    Poll the result of a large document submitted to /proxy/protect-document (over ~20,000 characters), processed asynchronously by a separate worker.

    POST
    /proxy/protect-retrieval

    Protect a batch of chunks retrieved from your vector store before they reach the LLM's context. Per-chunk role-based access control; fails closed on any detection error.

    POST
    /proxy/protect-image-document

    Protect a photographed or scanned document (national ID, passport, contract). OCR + detection + masking in one call, with an optional redacted copy of the image returned.

    GET
    /health

    Health check. Returns proxy status, version, and detector state.

    Input vs. output scanning

    Input scanning protects what goes into the model: /proxy/protect and /relay/complete detect and tokenise PII before the prompt reaches OpenAI, Anthropic or Gemini.

    Output scanning protects what comes back. On /relay/complete, /agent/protect and /proxy/protect-output the response is scanned and masked inline before it reaches your application, and audited with direction='output'.

    Limitation on streaming: on /relay/stream the output is audited in real time but cannot be masked — chunks are already delivered to the client before the scan completes. Use /relay/complete when masking of the response is required.

    AI Governance Platform: A 2026 Buyer's Guide

    September 2, 2026 9 min read

    "AI governance" now covers everything from model cards to prompt firewalls. If you are buying, the useful question is narrower: which controls actually sit in the request path between your applications and the model providers?

    The four layers of a real platform

    • Detection — regex plus NLP models that find PII, financial identifiers and contract clauses in prompts and completions.
    • Policy — rules per data type, role, org and provider, with actions: tokenize, anonymize or block.
    • Vault — reversible tokenization with encrypted originals and audited reveal.
    • Evidence — an immutable log of every interaction: entities detected, decision taken, user, timestamp.

    Tools that only produce documentation or dashboards fail the first audit question: show me the prompt that was sent to OpenAI.

    Evaluation criteria that matter

    1. Latency budget

    Inline scanning adds milliseconds to every call. Ask for p95 overhead with your own payload sizes, not a synthetic benchmark.

    2. Provider neutrality

    A governance layer that only supports one vendor becomes a migration blocker. Check OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini and self-hosted endpoints.

    3. Output scanning

    Most vendors scan prompts only. Models leak PII in completions too — from RAG context or memorized training data. Ask whether responses are scanned, and what happens with streaming: with SSE, masking mid-stream is not possible, so output scanning is audit-only unless you buffer the response.

    4. Multi-tenancy and roles

    Strict org separation, RBAC and DPO-scoped views are table stakes for regulated buyers.

    5. Exportable evidence

    Auditors want CSV and signed reports, not screenshots. Optional blockchain certification helps where non-repudiation is required.

    Common pitfalls

    • Buying a policy documentation tool and calling it enforcement.
    • Client-side redaction that any developer can bypass.
    • Irreversible anonymization where the workflow needs the original value back.
    • No plan for streaming responses.

    If you want the checklist applied to a concrete architecture, see the Privaro governance platform overview or the EU AI Act compliance guide.

    AI Compliance Software: What Auditors Actually Ask For

    September 5, 2026 7 min read

    Compliance software earns its budget on one day: the day an auditor, a customer's security team or a regulator asks for evidence. Everything else is preparation for that request.

    The five artifacts you will be asked for

    • Interaction log — every prompt and completion, with user, timestamp, provider and model.
    • Detection record — which sensitive entities were found, their type, severity and confidence.
    • Policy decision — what action was applied (tokenize, anonymize, block) and under which rule version.
    • Access trail — who revealed a tokenized value, when, and with what justification.
    • Retention proof — evidence that data was deleted on schedule.

    Why spreadsheets fail

    Manual registers drift within weeks of shipping. If the evidence is not produced by the same layer that enforces the control, the two disagree — and the auditor trusts neither.

    GDPR and EU AI Act overlap

    The GDPR asks about lawful basis, minimization, DPIA and transfers. The EU AI Act adds risk classification, technical documentation, logging and human oversight for high-risk systems. Both are satisfied by the same underlying record if your platform logs decisions rather than just traffic.

    Buying checklist

    • Are logs immutable and exportable (CSV, signed PDF)?
    • Can a DPO run a period report without engineering help?
    • Is reveal of tokenized data itself audited?
    • Are output detections logged, including streaming audit-only cases?
    • Is tenant isolation enforced at the database level (RLS), not in application code?

    GDPR Checklist for LLM Applications (2026)

    June 10, 2026 8 min read

    Every LLM feature you ship handles personal data — even if you did not intend it to. Users paste emails, contract clauses, internal IDs and customer names into prompts. Under the GDPR that is processing, and it triggers the same obligations as any other data flow in your product.

    This checklist condenses what a DPO will actually ask you before signing off on an LLM feature. Use it as an internal review template.

    1. Establish a lawful basis for prompt data

    Article 6 requires a lawful basis for every processing activity. For most B2B LLM features that means legitimate interest (documented via a balancing test) or contract when the feature is part of the service the customer paid for. Consent is rarely the right basis for an internal productivity tool.

    2. Apply data minimization at the proxy layer

    The single most effective control is to strip PII before the prompt reaches the model provider. This is where a PII detection API or a governance proxy like Privaro fits — every prompt gets scanned, entities get tokenized or masked, and only sanitized text hits OpenAI, Anthropic or Gemini.

    3. Run a DPIA for high-risk features

    Article 35 requires a Data Protection Impact Assessment when processing is likely to result in high risk. Any LLM feature that touches health, finance, legal or biometric data falls in scope. The DPIA should cover:

    • Categories of personal data flowing into prompts
    • Model provider and sub-processors (with SCCs on file)
    • Retention of prompts, completions and embeddings
    • Mitigations (tokenization, human review, opt-out)

    4. Lock down retention

    Model providers cache prompts. Vector databases retain embeddings. Log stores keep completions. Define a retention policy per surface and enforce it with automated deletion — do not rely on manual cleanup.

    5. Handle third-country transfers explicitly

    Most LLM providers process data in the US. You need Standard Contractual Clauses on file, and for sensitive categories a Transfer Impact Assessment. EU-region endpoints from Azure OpenAI or Anthropic on Bedrock EU can eliminate the transfer altogether — worth the migration for regulated verticals.

    6. Give data subjects a working DSAR path

    If a user requests deletion, you need to prove that their prompts, completions and derived embeddings are gone. That requires request-level audit logs from day one, not something you bolt on when the first DSAR arrives.

    EU AI Act Compliance for SaaS: What Ships in 2026

    May 22, 2026 9 min read

    The EU AI Act is the first horizontal AI regulation in force worldwide. If your SaaS serves EU customers, ships an LLM feature, or embeds a third-party model, you are in scope — regardless of where your company is headquartered.

    The four risk tiers, in plain English

    • Unacceptable — social scoring, manipulative AI. Banned.
    • High-risk — AI in hiring, credit scoring, medical devices, critical infrastructure. Heavy documentation and conformity assessment.
    • Limited risk — chatbots, generative AI. Transparency obligations (users must know they are interacting with AI).
    • Minimal risk — everything else. No specific obligations.

    Most SaaS LLM features land in limited risk, but a copilot that recommends candidates or scores loan applications moves straight into high-risk.

    GPAI: the model provider obligations that leak into you

    General-Purpose AI (GPAI) providers — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google — must maintain technical documentation, publish training data summaries and implement copyright policies. For you as a downstream deployer, this means:

    • Pin model versions and log them per request
    • Retain provider documentation with your DPIA
    • Notify users when GPAI output is used in decisions affecting them

    Transparency: the article 50 requirements

    Users interacting with an AI system must be informed. Content generated by AI (text, image, audio) must be marked as such in a machine-readable way. In practice this means adding disclosure UI to any user-facing generation surface and metadata to exported artifacts.

    The audit trail is the compliance product

    Enforcement will not ask for your policy document — it will ask for evidence. Every prompt, every model version, every policy decision, every human override must be logged in a way you can export to an auditor. This is the same requirement GDPR imposes for personal data, and the same one SOC 2 imposes for change management.

    A 90-day roadmap

    • Days 1–30: Inventory every LLM feature. Classify each into a risk tier.
    • Days 31–60: Deploy a governance proxy for PII detection, tokenization and per-request audit logs.
    • Days 61–90: Write the DPIA, publish the transparency notice, pin model versions.

    How to Mask PII Before Sending Prompts to OpenAI

    April 15, 2026 7 min read

    The fastest way to leak customer data is to forward a raw user prompt straight to OpenAI. This guide shows the pattern we recommend at Privaro: detect entities, replace them with reversible tokens, call the model, then re-hydrate the response.

    Why not just regex it?

    Regex catches email addresses and credit cards. It misses names, addresses, medical conditions, internal identifiers and anything context-dependent. Real PII detection needs a hybrid of regex, dictionaries and an NER model. Building that in-house is a 3-month project; the PII detection API gets you there in a day.

    The reversible tokenization pattern

    Four steps:

    • Detect — scan the prompt, return spans with entity type and confidence.
    • Tokenize — replace each span with a stable placeholder like [EMAIL_1]. Store the mapping encrypted in a vault, keyed to the request ID.
    • Send — forward the sanitized prompt to OpenAI. The model reasons about placeholders exactly like real values.
    • Rehydrate — on the response, swap placeholders back to originals before returning to the user.

    Minimal example

    const protect = await fetch("https://api.privaro.ai/v1/protect", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Authorization": `Bearer ${API_KEY}` },
  body: JSON.stringify({ text: userPrompt, policy: "strict" }),
});
const { safe_text, request_id } = await protect.json();

const completion = await openai.chat.completions.create({
  model: "gpt-4o",
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: safe_text }],
});

const rehydrate = await fetch("https://api.privaro.ai/v1/rehydrate", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Authorization": `Bearer ${API_KEY}` },
  body: JSON.stringify({ text: completion.choices[0].message.content, request_id }),
});
const { text } = await rehydrate.json();
return text;

    When to use irreversible anonymization instead

    Tokenization is right when you need to display the original values back to the end user. For analytics prompts, log summarization or training data preparation you want irreversible anonymization — the mapping is discarded and the data cannot be re-identified.

    What about latency?

    A well-designed proxy adds 40–80 ms per call. In practice that is invisible next to the 500–2000 ms of the LLM call itself, and it is the price of not leaking a customer's national ID into someone else's training set.

    AI Governance Tools in 2026: How to Choose One

    September 7, 2026 7 min read

    "AI governance" now labels four very different kinds of product. Buying the wrong category is the most common mistake we see in security reviews: a team purchases a policy documentation tool and discovers six months later that no prompt was ever inspected.

    The four categories

    • Policy and documentation platforms — registries of AI systems, risk classifications, model cards. They produce evidence, not enforcement.
    • Model evaluation and red-teaming — measure bias, toxicity and jailbreak resistance before release. Pre-production only.
    • Runtime gateways and proxies — sit on the request path, inspect prompts and responses, apply policies in real time. This is where Privaro sits.
    • Observability and cost tooling — latency, tokens, spend. Useful, but blind to personal data.

    Regulated teams usually need a runtime gateway plus a documentation layer. Evaluation matters when you fine-tune or ship your own models.

    Eight controls to check

    • Detection of PII, financial identifiers and contract data in prompts
    • Reversible tokenization with a controlled reveal path and access logs
    • Policies scoped by data type, user role, organization and provider
    • Scanning of model outputs, not just inputs
    • Per-request audit logs that survive a DSAR or a regulator's request
    • Provider-agnostic routing (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, self-hosted)
    • Strict multi-tenant separation and role-based access
    • Deployment options that keep data in your region

    Questions vendors dislike

    Ask what happens to a masked value when the model answers — can the original be restored, by whom, and is that reveal logged? Ask whether streaming responses are inspected, and what the tool can actually do mid-stream. Ask for a sample audit export and check that it names the entities detected, the policy applied and the decision, not just a timestamp.

    On streaming specifically, be sceptical of "we mask everything". Tokens leave the provider before any full sentence exists, so honest products describe server-sent-event streaming as audit-only and offer a non-streaming path when masking must be guaranteed.

    Build vs buy

    A regex layer in your own gateway covers card numbers and emails in an afternoon. It will not cover names, addresses, case references, tokenization with reveal control, per-tenant policies or exportable evidence.     PII in LLM Outputs: Why Input Filtering Is Not Enough

    September 7, 2026 6 min read

    Most teams start AI governance at the input: scan the prompt, mask what is sensitive, forward the rest. That closes the obvious hole and leaves a subtler one open — the model itself can produce personal data in its answer.

    Where output PII comes from

    • Retrieval: a RAG pipeline pulls a customer record into context and the model quotes it back
    • Tool calls: an agent queries an internal API and pastes the raw result into the response
    • Memorization: fine-tuned or long-context models reproduce training or session data
    • Reconstruction: the model infers and restates a masked value from surrounding context

    None of these are visible to an input-only filter. If the answer is then shown in a support console, emailed, or handed to another agent, the exposure is identical to sending the data to the provider in the first place.

    Two modes: shadow and enforce

    Turn output scanning on in shadow mode first: detections are logged, nothing is altered, and you get a real measurement of how often your pipelines emit personal data. Once the false-positive rate is acceptable, switch to enforce, where the configured action — mask, tokenize or block — is applied before the response reaches the user.

    The streaming limitation, stated honestly

    With server-sent events the provider emits tokens one by one and each token is already on its way to the client. A partial identifier can cross the wire before it is recognisable as one. Any vendor claiming full masking over SSE is describing buffering, which removes the reason to stream at all.

    The workable design is: SSE is audit-only — detections are recorded as incidents so a DPO can review them — and any flow that must guarantee masking uses a non-streaming call. In Privaro that means the relay endpoint for streaming and POST /v1/proxy/protect-output when the response must be sanitized before delivery.

    What to log

    An output incident is only useful if it records direction, entity types, the policy that matched, the action taken and whether the content actually reached the user. That last field is what separates "protected" from "leaked" in an audit, and it is the number your DPO will ask for.

    PII in RAG Pipelines: Protect at Ingest and at Retrieval

    September 21, 2026 7 min read

    Retrieval-augmented generation moves your documents into two new places: a vector index and, on every query, the model's context window. If personal data is in the source documents, it ends up in both — and most prompt filters never see it, because the sensitive text is injected by the retriever, not typed by the user.

    Two control points, not one

    • Ingest: before a document is chunked and embedded, detect and tokenize personal data so the index never stores raw values
    • Retrieval: before chunks are added to the prompt, scan them again and enforce who is allowed to see what

    Ingest protection shrinks the blast radius of the index itself. Retrieval protection handles everything ingest cannot: legacy indexes, documents that changed after indexing, and users who should not read every chunk the retriever finds relevant.

    Privaro Ingest

    POST /v1/proxy/protect-document accepts text, and the /upload variant accepts PDF, DOCX, XLSX, CSV and EML files. It returns the protected text plus the entity map, so you embed the sanitized version and keep originals in the encrypted token vault, reversible only through audited reveal.

    Privaro Retrieval Guard

    POST /v1/proxy/protect-retrieval receives the chunks your retriever selected and applies the pipeline policy to each one, with per-chunk access control. Chunks the caller should not see are dropped or masked before they reach the LLM, and every decision is logged against the request.

    Why embeddings of tokens still work

    Semantic search depends on meaning, not on the exact name or IBAN. Consistent tokens preserve structure ("[PERSON_1] signed the contract with [ORG_2]"), so retrieval quality stays close to the raw baseline while the index stops being a second copy of your customer database.

    Governing AI Agents: Why Monitoring Is No Longer Enough

    September 25, 2026 8 min read

    Enterprise AI has moved beyond isolated copilots. Agents now search internal knowledge, call business applications and pass information to other agents. As that footprint grows, organisations are discovering a basic problem: knowing that an agent exists does not tell you what data it can see, what it sends to a model or what it reveals in its answer.

    A 2026 Dataiku study conducted by Harris Poll among 685 CIOs found that 81% lack complete oversight of agents created outside approved systems. Seventy-two per cent cannot consistently measure whether all their agents deliver business outcomes, while 47% have already decommissioned more than 20 agents this year. These figures describe a visibility and accountability gap. They do not prove that every retired agent failed because of a security incident. Read the source study.

    The market is building a control layer

    Recent launches from governance, identity and security vendors show a common direction: enterprises need a control layer above fragmented agent platforms. Inventory, ownership, lifecycle status, cost and performance all belong in that layer. They answer important questions: which agents are running, who owns them and whether they are producing value.

    But visibility is not enforcement. A dashboard can show that an agent called a customer database. It cannot, by itself, prevent that agent from including an email address, an IBAN, a patient identifier or a contract value in a request to an external model.

    The missing question: what data crosses the boundary?

    Every agent sits at the intersection of identity, tools and data. Authentication answers who the agent is. Authorisation determines which system it may call. Runtime data governance determines what information may cross from that system into the model, and what may return to the user or the next agent.

    • Before the model call: detect sensitive entities in prompts, retrieved documents and tool results
    • At policy time: tokenize, anonymise or block according to data type, role, organisation and model provider
    • After the model call: inspect the response before it reaches a person, application or downstream agent
    • For audit: record the detection, policy decision, action, actor and timestamp for every interaction

    Why monitoring alone leaves a blind spot

    Tool access is not data permission

    An agent may be correctly authorised to query an ERP and still send more data than the task requires. Least-privilege access to a tool does not automatically create least-data disclosure inside each request.

    Prompt controls do not cover retrieval and output

    Sensitive content can enter through a RAG chunk or a tool response rather than the user's prompt. It can also appear in the model output. Controls therefore need to cover the full path, not only the initial message.

    An incident record is not preventive control

    Logs are essential evidence, but discovering an exposure after transmission is different from stopping it. Regulated workflows need both: inline enforcement to reduce risk and a traceable record to demonstrate what happened.

    A practical governance architecture

    Place a provider-neutral policy layer between enterprise applications or agents and the models they use. Route every interaction through the same sequence: detect, decide, protect, send, inspect and log. Reversible values belong in an encrypted token vault and should only be revealed through controlled, audited access. Organisation boundaries must remain strict throughout the flow.

    This complements agent inventory and performance management rather than replacing them. Together they answer both sides of governance: whether an agent should keep running, and whether each interaction respects the organisation's data policy while it runs.

    What security teams should ask next

    • Can we identify the sensitive data used in every agent interaction?
    • Are policies enforced before data reaches any model provider?
    • Do the same controls cover prompts, RAG context, tool results and outputs?
    • Can tokenized values be revealed only by authorised users with an audit trail?
    • Can we export evidence by agent, organisation, policy and provider?
